group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old woman presented to the emergency department in mid-winter after four days of progressive dyspnea, shaking chills, and a cough that started dry but became rust-colored overnight. She reported sleeping upright in a recliner because lying flat made it hard to catch her breath and produced a sharp, right-sided pleuritic pain. Earlier that morning she checked her home thermometer and noted 39.2 °C, prompting her daughter to drive her in. She denied confusion, syncope, seizure, or head trauma and was able to recount the timeline of her illness clearly on arrival. Past history is notable for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (last outpatient echocardiogram six months ago showed an EF of 35 %) managed with carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, and a stable low dose of furosemide, as well as chronic kidney impairment attributed to long-standing hypertension and type 2 diabetes; her most recent nephrology note documented an estimated glomerular filtration rate in the mid-40s mL/min/1.73 m². She has never required renal replacement therapy. Remote medical records list no strokes, malignancies, or chronic liver disorders. She lives in her own one-story house with her spouse, prepares her meals, and drives to weekly cardiac rehabilitation classes; she has had no hospital admissions or skilled-nursing stays in the past year. She quit smoking 15 years ago after a 25-pack-year exposure, consumes wine only on holidays, and denies illicit drug use. Immunizations include both pneumococcal vaccines within the past five years and the current season’s influenza shot. Before emergency medical personnel arrived she had taken only her morning medicines and a single 500 mg acetaminophen tablet, with no antibiotics or inhalers. On arrival, prior to any intervention, triage vitals were: oral temperature 39.2 °C, heart rate 103 beats per minute and regular, blood pressure 111/62 mm Hg in the right arm at heart level, respiratory rate 35 breaths per minute with moderate intercostal retractions, and oxygen saturation 88 % on ambient air that improved to 91 % when she was instructed to sit forward. She appeared flushed but alert, oriented to person, place, date, and situation, and conversed in complete sentences despite tachypnea. The skin was warm with brisk capillary refill. Jugular venous contour was at 5 cm above the sternal angle while upright, similar to her cardiology baseline. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 with a faint S3 but no new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary examination demonstrated dullness to percussion, decreased fremitus, and absent breath sounds over the right lower third posteriorly, with coarse crackles and bronchial breath sounds just superior to that zone; no wheezes were heard. The abdomen was soft and nontender, without hepatosplenomegaly or ascites. Extremities were warm, without edema or cyanosis, and distal pulses were 2 +. Neurologic screening showed equal pupils, intact extraocular movements, normal speech, and full strength throughout. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 128 mg/dL. Blood was drawn before any fluids, diuretics, or antimicrobials; initial laboratory results returned within 20 minutes revealed hematocrit 51 %, white blood cell count 15.2 × 10⁹/L with 88 % neutrophils, serum sodium 149 mEq/L, potassium 3.6 mEq/L, chloride 104 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 1.6). Venous lactate was 1.7 mmol/L. An arterial blood gas drawn on room air demonstrated pH 7.49, PaCO₂ 31 mm Hg, PaO₂ 71 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 23 mEq/L. A portable posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph obtained before any treatment showed a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and blunting of the right costophrenic angle accompanied by a 2-cm meniscus suggestive of an early parapneumonic fluid collection; the cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from prior imaging and there was no evidence of pulmonary vascular congestion. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 102 bpm with left ventricular hypertrophy criteria but no acute ischemic changes. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and a urinary pneumococcal antigen were obtained, and bedside lung ultrasound confirmed a small anechoic stripe layering above the right diaphragm consistent with pleural fluid. At the time of this note the patient had received no intravenous fluids, vasopressors, supplemental oxygen beyond ambient air for arterial sampling, diuretics, or antibiotics, allowing the above measurements to reflect her untreated physiologic state.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and imaging points at presentation.
- Demographics: woman aged 64 → 64 − 10 = 54. Lives at home, so no nursing-home points.
- Comorbidities: heart failure +10 and chronic renal disease +10. No malignancy, liver disease, or cerebrovascular disease: 0 each.
- Examination: respiratory rate 35/min (≥30) → +20. Alert mental status, systolic BP 111 (not <90), temperature 39.2°C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 103 (not ≥125) → 0 each.
- Laboratory findings: BUN 34 mg/dL (≥30) → +20. Arterial pH 7.49 (not <7.35), sodium 149 (not <130), glucose 128 (not ≥250), and hematocrit 51% (not <30%) → 0 each. Using the measured room-air arterial PaO₂ of 71 mm Hg, the <60 mm Hg criterion scores 0; the pulse oximetry reading is not scored separately.
- Imaging: confirmed pleural effusion → +10.
Total = 54 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 124 (risk class IV).
Final answer: 124
